headline: Job hugging: why nobody wants to quit anymore

sources.title: Half of workers are 'job hugging' - too scared to quit (Computerworld)
Job hugging: the growing trend of clinging to your job (The Week)
A new trend emerges in the economy. What is 'job hugging?' (video, CNN)

chunks.text: Something strange is happening at work: almost nobody is [[quitting]]. A few years ago, workers changed jobs quickly, chasing bigger [[paychecks]]. Now they {{hold on to}} their current jobs tightly, even jobs they do not love. Career experts call the new [[trend]] [[job hugging]]. Many workers {{settle for}} less money just to feel safe, and in one [[survey]], most said they plan to {{stick around}} rather than [[risk]] being the newest [[hire]] somewhere else.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose it
verbs.why: People hold on to a good job, and some hold on to old habits even when they no longer help. Many workers now hold on to their current jobs tightly, even ones they no longer enjoy.

verbs.correct: To accept less than you wanted
verbs.wrong: To demand more than you need
verbs.why: A buyer settles for a smaller house, and a runner sometimes settles for second place. Many workers now settle for less pay just to feel safe in their current job.

verbs.correct: To stay in a place longer
verbs.why: Friends stick around after a party ends, and fans stick around after the game for autographs. Most workers surveyed said they plan to stick around rather than risk being the newest hire somewhere else.

chunks.text: The reason is simple: the [[job market]] has [[cooled]]. The United States added just 73,000 jobs in July, far below last year's monthly [[average]] of about 111,000, and new [[openings]] are at their lowest level since 2023. When jobs {{dry up}}, moving feels dangerous, and news about [[layoffs]] makes the fear worse. Some people even {{turn down}} [[interviews]] for better-paying jobs, because leaving a safe seat feels like too big a [[bet]].

verbs.correct: To become smaller until almost gone
verbs.why: A river dries up during a drought, and funding for a project can dry up without warning. In today's job market, openings have dried up, and moving to a new job feels riskier than before.

verbs.correct: To say no to an offer
verbs.why: People turn down a job offer, turn down a party invitation, or turn down extra work. Some workers now even turn down interviews for better pay because leaving a safe job feels too risky.

chunks.text: But experts warn that [[comfort]] has a price. Workers who stop learning slowly {{fall behind}} the rest of their [[industry]]. Others {{burn out}} in [[roles]] they no longer enjoy but feel too nervous to leave. One large [[consulting firm]] says people are now hugging their jobs [[for dear life]]. And that is the problem: in the long run, fear can {{hold back}} a whole career.

verbs.correct: To fail to keep the same pace
verbs.wrong: To move ahead of the group
verbs.why: Students fall behind in class after missing a few weeks, and workers fall behind on new skills without regular training. Employees who stop learning slowly fall behind the rest of their industry.

verbs.correct: To become too tired to continue
verbs.wrong: To get angry at a coworker
verbs.why: Nurses burn out after years of long shifts, and students burn out during exam season. Some workers now burn out in jobs they no longer enjoy but feel too nervous to leave.

verbs.wrong: To push something to go faster
verbs.why: Fear can hold back a talented worker, and doubt can hold back a good idea. Experts warn that in the long run, fear can hold back a person's whole career.

chunks.text: So what should a job hugger do? The advice is not to quit tomorrow. It is to stay active inside the hug. Workers can {{branch out}} into new skills, join small [[projects]] in other teams, and quietly {{look around}} for openings elsewhere, even if they never [[apply]]. It is fine to [[play it safe]] for now. But when the market improves again, the best jobs will go to the people who never stopped learning, even inside their [[comfort zone]].

verbs.correct: To try new and different things
verbs.why: A bakery might branch out into wedding cakes, and a writer might branch out into new topics. Workers today can branch out into new skills and join small projects on other teams.

verbs.wrong: To rest before a big change
verbs.why: Shoppers look around before buying, and buyers look around at several houses before choosing one. Job huggers can quietly look around at other openings without ever applying.

mainIdea.s: Workers in a slow job market are keeping the jobs they already have instead of changing companies. Experts call it job hugging and warn that too much safety has costs.
mainIdea.why: With openings at their lowest since 2023, people hold on to jobs tightly, but skills can fall behind and fear can hold back a career.

mainIdea.s: Workers are staying at their companies because bosses now pay big loyalty bonuses every year. Experts say the rewards have finally ended decades of constant job hopping.
mainIdea.why: Close, but people are staying out of fear, not because of bonuses. Many even settle for less money just to feel safe.

mainIdea.s: Millions of employees quit their jobs together this summer to protest low pay across many industries. The government expects the wave of quitting to continue all year.
mainIdea.why: It is the opposite. Almost nobody is quitting, because new openings have dried up and change feels risky.

tf.s: Workers are holding on to jobs they do not even love
tf.why: Career experts call the trend job hugging. Changing jobs feels too risky in a cool market.

tf.s: The United States added more jobs in July than the average last year
tf.why: July added just 73,000 jobs, far below the earlier monthly average of about 111,000.

tf.s: Some people turn down interviews for better-paying jobs
tf.why: Leaving a safe seat feels like too big a bet, so they say no even to good chances.

tf.s: Experts say workers who stop learning can fall behind their industry
tf.why: That is the price of comfort. Others burn out in roles they feel too nervous to leave.

tf.s: The article's advice is to quit your job tomorrow
tf.why: The advice is to stay active: branch out into new skills and quietly look around for openings.

tf.s: The report says job openings are at their highest level in years
tf.why: Openings are at their lowest level since 2023, which is why moving feels so dangerous.
